loading.status_physics: Preparing the Monte Carlo physics simulation

0.s: The electric field leaving a closed surface is set by the charge inside it. The more charge, the stronger the field escaping out through the surface.

1.s: Magnetic field lines always connect and have neither a start nor an end. That is why there are no magnetic monopoles: a north pole always arrives packed with a south pole.

2.s: The gravitational potential at a point is the sum of every nearby mass contributing. Each piece of mass plays its part, and the farther it sits, the smaller its effect.

3.s: Stress inside a material is a tensor, so its value depends on the axes you choose. This formula moves the stress components into another coordinate system using the rotation matrix Q.

4.s: Temperature changes for two reasons: carried along by the flow (advection) and spread through conduction (diffusion), plus any heat source. This equation folds all three together.

graph.title: 3D Graph

graph.hint_gfractal: Mandelbrot, Julia (set c) and Newton (roots of z³-1). Drag = pan, scroll = zoom. Raise iterations for detail.

graph.hint_gslope: Slope field y'=f(x,y). Click anywhere to draw an RK4 solution from that point. Drag = pan, scroll = zoom.
graph.hint_gdist: Distribution PDF/CDF with live parameters and highlighted P(a≤X≤b) area. Sliders change parameters instantly.
graph.hint_ggraphalgo: Random weighted graph. Pick an algorithm and watch animated steps (gold = visited, bright = path/MST). Nodes are draggable.
graph.hint_gfield: Charges are draggable; gold lines = equipotentials, arrows = E field direction. Arrow length ∝ field strength.
graph.hint_gpvcycle: P-V diagram of Carnot/Otto/Diesel cycles with animated state point. Efficiency is computed from the parameters.
graph.hint_gising: 2D Ising model via Metropolis. Lower T below Tc≈2.27 to watch domains merge (magnetization rises).
graph.hint_gminkowski: Minkowski diagram: light cone, moving-frame axes and calibration hyperbola. Drag events to see invariant s².
graph.hint_gfluid: 2D fluid simulation (Jos Stam). Drag to inject ink and velocity; the dye follows the velocity field.
graph.hint_ggeodesic: Geodesics in the Schwarzschild metric (rs=1). Photons with b<1.5 are captured; large b get deflected. Massive orbits can precess.
graph.hint_gray: Two thin lenses with parallel incoming rays. Thin-lens formula applied at each surface. Negative f = concave lens.

catalog.b: A set of ready-made experiments. Each item auto-fills the surface shape, field, and domain, then you are free to tweak everything afterwards. ELI5: like a set menu at a restaurant, just pick one, then modify it to taste.

surface.b: The "topography" of the surface the electric field passes through. ELI5: imagine a sheet of fabric pulled up and down; f(x,y) is the height of that fabric at every point (x,y). A flat surface means f = 0, a hill means f = exp(-x^2-y^2), etc. Mathematically it's called a 2D manifold in 3D space.

domain.b:
The stretch of ground beneath the surface where Monte Carlo "rolls dice" to place sample points. Units are meters (SI), so the domain area dx·dy is directly in m².
ELI5: this is the map of the area you pick for the experiment; the wider it is, the more flux gets caught.

field.b:
The electric field is the "wind" that pushes a small +1 C charge. Its unit is N/C (newtons per coulomb), the same as V/m.
ELI5: if you place a 1 C charge at a point, a 500 N/C field means it is pushed or pulled with 500 newtons.

fieldmode.b:
Uniform: same strength & direction everywhere, like a constant wind, easy to reason about, great for learning basic flux.
Point charge: the field spreads radially from a single charge, strength falls off as 1/r² (Coulomb's law).
Custom formula: write your own field components P, Q, R as functions of x, y, z.

strength.b:
How "hard" the field is, in newtons per coulomb.
ELI5: think of E₀ as rain thickness (heavy vs light drizzle). Reference points: overcast weather ~100 N/C, indoors ~100 to 300 N/C, a lightning storm can reach thousands of N/C. The stronger the field, the more flux pierces the surface (Φ ∝ E).

direction.b: The direction of the 3D electric-field arrow. ELI5: rain can fall straight onto your head (+z), slanted from the front, or from the side. Flux is largest when the field is perpendicular to the surface; if the field is parallel to it (just sliding along), the flux is zero because nothing "gets through". The formula Φ uses the field component that runs along the surface normal.

charge.b:
The size of the point charge that acts as the field's source, in nano-coulombs (10⁻⁹ C). The field is E = kQ/r² with k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C².
ELI5: a charge is like a water tap; the bigger Q, the harder the field pours out. 5 nC is still "safe", but remember 5 C is enormous (lightning level).

chargepos.b:
Location of the source charge in meters. Important: don't put it on (or inside) the surface, the 1/r² field explodes to infinity, and Monte Carlo can become invalid.
ELI5: keep the electric balloon up in the air, not stuck onto the middle of the surface.

customfield.b:
A free-form vector field: E = ⟨P, Q, R⟩ as functions of (x,y,z), in N/C. Examples: ⟨−y, x, 0⟩ is a rotating field; ⟨0, 0, 1⟩ is a wind pointing up; a point charge at (0,0,2): ⟨k(x−x₀), k(y−y₀), k(z−z₀)⟩/r³ (wire it yourself).
ELI5: this is the pro control panel: you can bend the field into any shape you like, as long as it's in N/C.

flip.b:
Flux carries a sign that depends on the surface orientation. A +z normal means "outward, upward".
ELI5: like choosing to face a window inward or outward: rain coming in is +, going out is −. The total Φ flips sign, but "how much" field pierces through stays the same in size.

mc.b:
Instead of computing a symbolic integral (hard for complicated surfaces), we throw N random points over the domain, add up each point's flux contribution g = −P·fₓ − Q·f_y + R, then average: Φ ≈ (domain area)·mean(g).
ELI5: want to know how much rain lands in a weirdly shaped garden? Scatter N random buckets over the whole garden, measure them, then average.

samples.b:
How many random points. Error shrinks like ~1/√N: 100× more N only makes the error 10× smaller.
ELI5: the more dice throws, the closer the result gets to the truth. 100,000 throws is usually accurate to about 0.3%; need very high accuracy? raise N.

seed.b:
The starting number of the random machine. With the same seed, the simulation can be repeated exactly.
ELI5: like a film you can rewind: the experiment becomes scientifically reproducible. Leave it empty if you want a different result each run.

ai.b:
You write a free-form scenario → the text is sent to an LLM (OpenRouter, key in config.json) → the AI returns a JSON configuration (surface, field, domain, flux direction) → the backend validates the formulas & numbers mathematically (the AI cannot inject code) → the parameters fill the form → the Monte Carlo simulation runs on the Python module.
ELI5: the AI is a clever typist assistant; the one doing the actual math is still the physics calculator in the backend.

matrix.hint: Use the field's menu (Insert matrix) for any NxN matrix, then fill the cells with numbers.

ode.hint: Use y' and y'' for derivatives. Example: y'' + y = sin(x)

hydro.use3: P_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^{2} + \rho g h_1 = P_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^{2} + \rho g h_2

poly.hint: Type the whole polynomial p(x) above, e.g. x^2 - 5x + 6, then choose roots or factorisation. Operators like the definite integral are evaluated first automatically.

gr.hint: Leave r empty to compute the radius only. r must be larger than the Schwarzschild radius.

heatexp.use3: Q = m\,L \;\text{(phase change without temperature rise)}

gsurf3d.use2: \text{tangent plane: } z = f_0 + f_x\Delta x + f_y\Delta y

gdist.use1: P(a \le X \le b) = \text{area under the PDF}

sims.lg_hint: Logistic map x(k+1) = r·x(k)(1−x(k)). Raise r slowly: fixed point → period 2 → 4 → chaos. Lyapunov exponent > 0 = chaos.
sims.lz_hint: Lorenz system via RK4. Defaults σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3 = the classic butterfly attractor. ρ < 24.74 converges to a fixed point.
sims.fo_hint: f is evaluated numerically on [−L, L] (N max 60). Try f(x)=x, |x|, or x². Coefficients via trapezoid quadrature.
sims.mx_hint: Fill the 2×2 matrix cells. Plot: unit circle → ellipse, unit square → parallelogram, arrows = basis e₁,e₂ and their images.
sims.w_hint: Random unit steps (uniform angle), the seed fixes the outcome, same seed, same result. Theoretical RMS = √steps.
sims.dp_hint: RK4 Δt = 0.002 s. Energy is conserved (drift ~1e-7%). Large angles = chaos: try θ₁ = 170°.
sims.dr_hint: RK4 with quadratic drag F = ½ρCₑAv². Dashed curve = vacuum. Defaults = a baseball.
sims.ke_hint: μ = GM (free units). Starts at perihelion with vis-viva speed. Compare the measured period with Kepler's Third Law.
sims.sl_hint: On-screen intensity: I = cos²(πdy/λL) × sinc²(πay/λL). a = 0 → ideal double slit.
sims.qm_hint: Natural units ħ = m = 1. A Gaussian packet hits a square barrier; split-step Fourier integration. Norm is conserved.

sslit.use1: I(y) = \cos^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi d y}{\lambda L}\right) \cdot \mathrm{sinc}^{2}\!\left(\dfrac{\pi a y}{\lambda L}\right)
